title: Australia in recession: biggest contraction since the Great Depression, ABS confirms
summary: The model case of a pandemic-driven technical recession: shows which parts of aggregate demand collapsed, how the savings ratio jumped and how Australia compared with other advanced economies.
lede: GDP fell 7 per cent in the June quarter 2020, confirming Australia's first recession since 1990-91 with the economy 6.3 per cent smaller over the year. Household consumption collapsed as restrictions closed services, while JobKeeper pushed the profit share above 30 per cent.

figures.label: Contribution of private demand to GDP
GDP, June quarter 2020: United States / UK / Germany / Canada

terms.def: Two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth.
Household savings as a share of household disposable income.
Real GDP divided by population; a rough guide to income per person.

angle: Use the component breakdown (consumption -12.7%, private demand -7.9 points, net trade +1.0 point) to show which parts of AD drove the contraction, then contrast with the Great Depression and with other economies.

questions.q: Identify two components of aggregate demand that contributed to the fall in GDP in the June quarter 2020, using the article.
Explain why the household savings ratio rose to 19.8 per cent during the June quarter 2020.
Using data from the article, assess the severity of Australia's contraction relative to other advanced economies.

extended: Analyse the effects of an economic downturn on households, businesses and the government.
note: Older item (published Sep 2020): figures are as at that date; check for newer data before quoting. Newspaper article reproduced for classroom use. Headline and a quarterly-fall figure of 7 per cent are as reported by the newspaper; confirm in the ABS National Accounts.

title: Far from bouncing back, China's economy may be shrinking
summary: Shows why official statistics can mislead and how COVID-19 disrupted the world's growth locomotive, with consequences for Australia's export demand and the global business cycle.
lede: Peter Hartcher argues official claims that China is back to normal are unreliable, citing reports of faked electricity use and propped-up share markets. Independent indicators and economist Bert Hofman suggest weak consumer activity and 2020 growth of 2 to 4.5 per cent, below Beijing's 6 per cent goal.

title: Economic brief: the effects of sustained budget deficits
summary: A one-page summary of the budget deficit, net debt and bond-financing effects of the COVID-19 fiscal response, with a simple T and G diagram.
lede: Tim Riley explains that the 2019-20 budget moved from a forecast surplus of $7.1b to a deficit of $14b or more as tax revenue fell and spending rose. Net debt was forecast at $361b and could exceed $500b, funded by Australian Government Securities.

terms.def: Government spending (G) exceeds tax revenue (T).
Government borrowings less financial assets.
Higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

angle: Use the deficit and net debt figures to explain the cost of an expansionary stance and how deficits are financed by selling bonds.

questions.q: Explain how a fall in income can move the budget from surplus to deficit.
Outline one effect of sustained budget deficits on the Australian economy.

title: Economic forecasts, April/May 2020: key indicators at the start of the COVID-19 recession
summary: A one-page dashboard of GDP, inflation, unemployment, wages, current account, interest rates and the exchange rate in the first months of the pandemic.
lede: Table of latest figures and forecasts compiled from ABS, RBA and Budget sources. It shows unemployment jumping 1 percentage point to 6.2 per cent in April 2020, the cash rate cut to 0.25 per cent and the Australian dollar falling to US$0.55 in March before stabilising at US$0.64.

title: Economy had more momentum: stronger retail growth in December quarter
summary: Shows how stronger consumption led economists to abandon calls for another rate cut just before COVID-19 changed the outlook.
lede: Retail trade rose 0.5 per cent in real terms in the December quarter 2019, above the 0.3 per cent expected. Economists said the RBA, holding the cash rate at 0.75 per cent, was unlikely to cut again, although bushfires and coronavirus posed new risks.

title: Fiscal measures in response to the COVID-19 pandemic
summary: A full account of the three 2020 fiscal packages, JobKeeper and the budget consequences; usable as the Australian fiscal case study for the downturn.
lede: Describes the supply and demand shocks from COVID-19 and the three fiscal phases: $17.63b on 12 March, $66.1b on 22 March and the $130b JobKeeper wage subsidy on 30 March. Total support reached $320b (16.4 per cent of GDP) and the budget moved from a forecast surplus of $7.1b to a deficit of at least $14b.

angle: Use it to describe the discretionary expansion of fiscal policy in 2020 and to separate cyclical from structural parts of the deficit.

title: How millennials could make the Fed's job harder
summary: Links saving behaviour, the paradox of thrift, low inflation expectations and the limited room for central banks to cut rates.
lede: Jeanna Smialek reports that aggressive saving and low inflation expectations among young people could leave the US Federal Reserve with less room to cut interest rates. With US rates at 1.5 to 1.75 per cent, the Fed has room for about six quarter-point cuts, compared with rates above 5 per cent before the last recession.

title: Learning to live without inflation
summary: Explains why very low inflation keeps interest rates low and what that means for savers, using the real versus nominal rate distinction.
lede: Ross Gittins argues that interest rates are low mainly because inflation has fallen for 30 years, not because of the pandemic, so retirees must adjust. CPI rose only 0.7 per cent over the year to September 2020, and self-funded retirees' living costs also rose 0.7 per cent.

title: Microeconomic reform policies
summary: Teaching notes covering the rationale, examples, efficiency gains and costs of microeconomic reform, with an AD-AS diagram and a timeline of Australian reforms.
lede: Tim Riley sets out how reform shifts aggregate supply to the right, with examples in product and factor markets such as tariff cuts, the National Competition Policy, the GST, financial deregulation and enterprise bargaining. It lists the costs, including structural unemployment and reform fatigue, and cites the Productivity Commission on stalled productivity.

title: Seize the day for tax reform
summary: A well-argued case for broad tax reform as part of the COVID-19 recovery, with specific proposals on GST, cash-flow taxes, stamp duty and road pricing.
lede: John Hewson argues the tax and transfer system is too complex, inefficient and unfair and that the pandemic offers a chance to reform it. He says lifting the GST rate to about 15 per cent and broadening it could raise $90 billion to $100 billion a year, a third of which would compensate the bottom 40 per cent of earners.

title: The Reserve Bank's recent conduct of monetary policy
summary: A full account of the RBA's March 2020 package, with a table of 17 cash rate cuts since 2011 and the RBA's May 2020 baseline scenario.
lede: The RBA cut the cash rate to 0.25 per cent on 20 March 2020, set a 0.25 per cent target for 3-year bond yields, created a funding facility of at least $90b and raised the interest on exchange settlement balances to 0.10 per cent. On 5 May it held policy settings and outlined a baseline with GDP down about 6 per cent in 2020 and unemployment peaking near 10 per cent.

title: Weak inflation tells us: it's the demand side, stupid
summary: Explains deflation and the case for fiscal policy when interest rates are near zero, using the June quarter 2020 CPI fall.
lede: Ross Gittins explains that the 1.9 per cent fall in the CPI in the June quarter 2020 reflected cuts to childcare and petrol prices, not deflation. Inflation has been below the RBA's target for almost six years, so he argues monetary policy is exhausted and fiscal policy must support demand.

title: What is a recession?
summary: Defines technical recession and the alternative unemployment-based definition, and records Australia's past recessions.
lede: Jessica Irvine explains that a technical recession is two quarters of negative GDP growth and that Saul Eslake prefers a rise in unemployment of 1.5 percentage points within 18 months. December quarter 2019 GDP was $480.4 billion, up 0.5 per cent, and the first stimulus package was $17.6 billion.

title: Why a trade war would be dumb
summary: Gives the free-trade argument against retaliating when China restricts Australian exports, with comparative advantage and tariff reform history.
lede: Jessica Irvine argues Australia should not retaliate with tariffs against China's restrictions on exports such as barley, beef, wine and lobsters. She says tariffs would be illegal under WTO rules, escalate tensions and raise prices for Australian shoppers, and that tariff reduction since the Whitlam government has lifted productivity and wages.

summary: Explains how the CPI is built (basket, weights, frequency) and why it understates pressure on households with mortgages.
lede: Millie Muroi explains that the CPI is a rough estimate of price changes that excludes interest rates, and that inflation was 2.4 per cent in the year to December 2024, the slowest since March 2021. Working households' living costs rose 4.7 per cent against 2.8 per cent for self-funded retirees.
